speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Thereafter, Second Minister for Finance Ms Indranee Rajah will address Parliamentary Question Nos 6 and 7, as well as Written Question No 20 in today's Order Paper.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I will provide an overview of the drivers of inflation, the outlook ahead, as well as how inflation is being managed.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Second Minister for Finance will then address the questions relating to the Government's fiscal and household support measures.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, the world economic recovery has raised the demand for energy and pushed up global energy prices even as supply remains tight.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, global food commodity inflation is climbing as global demand grows amid the supply constraints that is caused by climate change, weather-related disruptions and labour shortages in key food-producing countries.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Third, supply bottlenecks in key global industries and transport hubs have exacerbated cost pressures, including higher logistics costs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, inflation in the US climbed to 6.8% on a year-on-year basis in November last year, its highest in 39 years.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In the Eurozone, inflation in November 2021 was 4.9%, the highest in 25 years.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In Asia, South Korea's inflation hit a decade-high of 3.8% in November.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: As a small and open economy that imports most of our items, we are subject to these global economic forces as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The rise in domestic inflation comes largely on the back of external inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Items like petrol, electricity and gas, as well as food prices and imported products are affected by the global drivers I have just described.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Besides global forces contributing to this northward trend, there are domestic factors at play too, for instance, accommodation and private transport costs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Car prices have been rising at a faster rate due to bigger reductions in the Certificate of Entitlement (COE) quotas and the continuing strong demand for cars.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Due to construction delays brought on by COVID-19, the need for rental housing has edged up.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, as accommodation costs comprise mainly of imputed rentals on owner-occupied accommodation and most Singaporeans live in owner-occupied homes and use public transport, these two factors are not likely to apply to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Hence, a more useful gauge of inflation which excludes these two items is the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Core Inflation rate, which is so far, lower than the headline inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While MAS Core Inflation has moved up from 0.4% year-on-year in the first half of 2021 to 1.1% in the third quarter of last year, and to 1.6% last November, it is still lower than the headline inflation of 2.5% and 3.8% over the same period.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In the near term, Singapore is likely to continue to face external cost pressures.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is due to global energy prices remaining elevated and bottlenecks in global transportation, as well as supply-demand mismatches in various commodities and goods markets, which are likely to persist for a while.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: However, the Ministry of Trade and Information (MTI) and MAS expect these rises to be temporary and pressures to ease gradually over the course of the year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In particular, global oil prices should ease as production increases to catch up with demand.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: On our domestic labour front, wage growth is likely to continue to improve as the demand for labour strengthens on the back of a continued pick-up in economic activity.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government’s roll-out of Progressive Wage policies such as the expansion of the Progressive Wage Model to the retail sector would also support wages for lower-wage Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: At the same time, as the COVID-19 situation stabilises, consumer demand should improve.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: With all these factors in mind, MAS Core Inflation is expected to increase in the first half of 2022, before easing in the later part of the year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI and MAS will carefully monitor price trends over the next few months of the year closely, before revising the forecasts if necessary.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the second-round effects of inflation and whether it will persist.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI and MAS's assessment is that while household inflation expectations have risen slightly, they remain well-anchored.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In particular, household expectations of inflation have remained below historical averages.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Hence, MTI and MAS do not expect persistent, accelerating inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Shawn Huang asked about the forward-looking inflation indicators that are being monitored.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Both MTI and MAS monitor a range of upstream cost indicators to form a forward-looking view of inflationary pressures in the economy.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We closely follow external indicators like the global commodity prices reflected by the Brent crude oil benchmark, as well as international food commodity price indices and import prices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Domestic indicators consist of business cost measures such as resident wages and commercial rentals.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: While the small and open nature of our economy constrains how much we can shield Singaporeans from inflationary pressures, the Government will spare no effort to lessen its impact.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We have put in place a multi-pronged strategy to mitigate inflationary pressures.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: First, the Government is striving hard to keep the Singapore economy competitive, so that we keep creating good jobs for Singaporeans and to bring sustainable wage growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For example, before the pandemic, from 2014 to 2019, Singapore's economy was expanding by 3.1% per annum on average.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Even though the pandemic led to the economy contracting by 5.4% in 2020, it rebounded by 7.2% last year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The strong recovery has helped to ensure that resident workers enjoyed real wage growth in 2021, after accounting for inflation.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Specifically, we note that in 2021, the real median income growth of full-time employed residents was positive, at 1.1%.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the potential impact of inflation on Singapore's economic growth this year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI's assessment is that Singapore's economic recovery remains on track, with the GDP expected to grow by 3% to 5% this year.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This should continue to support recovery in the labour market in the year ahead.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Second, given the imported and domestic cost pressures, MAS tightened the monetary policy in October last year by shifting the trade-weighted Singapore dollar towards an appreciating path.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Since then, the Singapore dollar has strengthened, which will help reduce the Singapore dollar cost of imports and shield Singaporeans from some of the external cost pressures.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: For instance, the Singapore dollar has appreciated significantly against the currencies of the country's major food sources over the longer term, and this has moderated the pass-through effects of external inflationary pressure.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Third, the Government carefully manages domestic supply-side constraints, such as the supply of industrial and commercial space, to help rein in business rental costs that may translate to higher consumer prices.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: During the pandemic, businesses received rental relief to cope with their rental costs.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Additionally, policy measures, such as the Wage Credit Scheme, Jobs Support Scheme and Jobs Growth Incentive Scheme, have alleviated the labour outlay of businesses.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Fourth, the Government has been diversifying our food import sources and today, our food supplies come from more than 170 countries and regions from the world.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This helps to ensure that the prices of our food supplies remain competitive and reduce our vulnerability to larger price fluctuations globally.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: MTI and the various Ministries and agencies want to thank our industry partners, including our trade associations and key supermarket retailers who have been working closely with us, especially in the last two years, to diversify and secure alternate food sources for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Fifth, the Government works closely with industry partners, including major retailers, to ensure that the prices of daily necessities and food items are competitive and affordable.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether there are further plans to enhance cooperation with retailers this year on daily necessities and food items.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Some retailers like NTUC FairPrice have helped to keep the prices of essential items affordable.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: It has extended its discount schemes for seniors and low-income families by another year to cover the whole of this year, 2022.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: This is estimated to result in more than S$11 million worth of savings for customers, covering Pioneer Generation and Merdeka Generation seniors, as well as the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) blue cardholders.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Another initiative is the Government's effort to work with the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) to onboard more retailers onto its Price Kaki app.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The app is for consumers, and it promotes price transparency and helps consumers make informed choices by providing easy and timely comparisons of the prices of groceries and hawker food.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Government provides targeted assistance to lower-income Singaporeans who need support for their basic living expenses through schemes such as the permanent GST Voucher scheme, Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) rebates and the Public Transport Vouchers.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: The Second Minister for Finance will elaborate on these in her response.
